title: The N-th Number Built From Given Primes
statement:
`primes` is a list of different prime numbers in increasing order. A positive whole number is **smooth** for these primes if every prime factor it has is in the list; `1` counts (it has no prime factors). For `primes = [3, 5]` the smooth numbers in increasing order are `1, 3, 5, 9, 15, 25, 27, 45, ...`.

Return the `n`-th smooth number (counting from 1). It is guaranteed to fit in a 32-bit signed integer.
constraints: 1 <= len(primes) <= 10, each prime is at most 100

expected.time: O(n * k) or O(n * k log n)

hints.nudge: Every smooth number except 1 is a smaller smooth number times one of the primes. How can you produce the smooth numbers in increasing order without testing every integer?
hints.pattern: A min-heap of candidates: pop the smallest, push its products with every prime (skipping numbers already pushed). Or one pointer per prime into the list built so far, taking the smallest candidate each step.
hints.pseudocode:
smooth = [1]; pointer[j] = 0 for every prime j
repeat n - 1 times:
  next = the smallest of primes[j] * smooth[pointer[j]] over all j
  append next to smooth
  for every j with primes[j] * smooth[pointer[j]] == next: pointer[j] += 1
return smooth[n - 1]
hints.walkthrough: Testing every integer for smoothness is hopeless when the answer is near 2 * 10^9. Build the numbers in order instead. Each smooth number is an earlier smooth number multiplied by a prime from the list. With a min-heap: start with 1; pop the smallest x (the next smooth number), push x * p for each prime p (use a set so that a number reached in two ways, like 3 * 5 and 5 * 3, is pushed once). With pointers: for each prime keep the position of the earliest smooth number that, multiplied by this prime, has not been used yet; the next smooth number is the smallest of these products, and every pointer whose product equals it moves forward (this also removes duplicates). The pointer version is O(n * k) with no heap.
